claim: On 490 mostly human-crowd items (capitals, trivia, dermatology, art) the surprisingly popular (SP) rule cut errors 21.3% vs majority vote (sign test P<0.0005). The pooled gain comes mostly from the capitals studies (48% cut); on trivia it was 14% (P=.031).
agent_test: Run SP vs majority on a fixed question set at equal token budget: N answer samples plus N predictions of what share of other samples will give each answer; compare error rates with a paired sign test.

claim: SP beat confidence-weighted vote by 24.2% on the 290-item subset (P=0.0107) but not max-confidence (22.2%, P<0.13).
agent_test: Add a confidence-weighted and a max-confidence arm to the SP test.

claim: SP works by exploiting the gap between actual and predicted vote share; holders of a correct rare view predict a smaller share for their answer than naive majority holders do.
agent_test: Check in LLM samples whether answers with a correct minority view receive lower predicted share from their own holders (log vote/prediction pairs).
audit_note: Wikipedia is a secondary summary of Prelec, so only one independent source; claim is a method description so this does not matter.

claim: SP needs predictions that are informative and spread out. When most predictions sit near 50-50 (81% of items in the trivia study) SP rarely changes the majority and its gain shrinks.
agent_test: Record the share of predictions near 50/50 per task; test whether SP gain falls with that share.

claim: The theory needs a shared prior, conditionally independent signals and honest reports; with 50 items and 30 respondents SP reaches P<0.05 against majority in only about 40% of simulated studies (392/1000), so single small studies are underpowered.
agent_test: Use at least a few hundred items when comparing SP to majority.

claim: Human replication on real forecasting tasks is mixed: college football (216 games) SP 51.4% vs majority 53.9% (SP worst); NBA (465 games) SP 67.3% vs majority 65.9%; midterm races SP 80.0% vs majority 79.1%; among objectively assessed experts SP 60.2% / 82.7% vs majority 59.0% / 79.6% (football / elections). Differences are small and not shown to be significant.
agent_test: Not needed; use as a prior that SP gain over majority is small outside Prelec's own designs.

claim: SP is helped when respondents include real experts; with mostly non-experts (6 of 227 self-rated expert in football) the gain disappears. Self-assessed experts did worse under SP (71.8%) than under majority (77.3%) on elections.
agent_test: For LLMs, vary sample diversity (different personas or models) and see when SP helps.

claim: In a separate study of 256 football games SP (68%, 174 correct) edged the mode (172.5), confidence-weighted (166) and most of 94 media experts; small margin on one season.
agent_test: none

claim: Meta-prediction can weight respondents (extremised meta-prediction weighting): +6.64 points over simple average (95% CI 5.61-7.63) on 500 science true/false items, about +9 on the hardest level, nothing at the easiest.
agent_test: Weight LLM samples by how well each sample predicts the others' answers; compare with plain majority.

claim: For ranking tasks, combining votes with predictions recovers rankings far better than either alone (each near random; random top-of-4 error 0.75) and beat Borda, Copeland, IRV and others. Partial-preference SP also works with under 20% fitted experts.
agent_test: For multi-option outputs, elicit top-k plus predicted top-k of other samples and compare to Borda.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: For LLM ensembles, correlated errors break SP. On five models and four binary benchmarks (375,000 responses) SP gave no consistent gain over single-sample: HLE (35 questions, T=1.0) SP was above majority for one Qwen3 model (20.2 to 25.4) but below for another (25.1 to 22.8); Com2Sense majority and SP both far below single-sample for three of four models. Over 19 model-benchmark cells at T=1.0, SP vs majority: 9 wins, 9 losses, 1 tie. Top wrong answer was 65-87% of wrong responses on MATH.
agent_test: Measure error correlation across the scaffold's own samples first; apply SP only where wrong answers are diverse.

claim: Models are better at predicting what other models will say than at identifying what is true, and aggregation methods including Surprisingly Popular gave no reliable gain over a single sample (Denisov-Blanch et al. 2026); separately, LLMs systematically favour popular options and pick a popular wrong answer 66% of the time when all distractors are more popular than the correct one (Abdallah et al. 2026), which would plausibly hurt SP when the popular answer is wrong, but SP was not tested there.
agent_test: Build items where the wrong answer is the common one and compare SP, majority and a verifier.
audit_note: Consensus-is-not-verification does report models predict other models better than truth and SP/aggregation failing; the popularity paper (arXiv 2608.29257) never tests SP, so 'both make SP fail' is an inference, not a finding.
claim_before_audit: Models predict what other models say better than they identify truth, and models favour popular options; both make SP fail when the popular answer is wrong (66% popular-wrong choices when all distractors are more popular).

claim: A learned inverse surprising popularity (ISP) with four simulated agents (accuracy 0.6-0.9) beats majority (91.37 vs 85.13 at K=2) while plain SP is worse than majority (79.94). On real LLM ensembles ISP beat majority by about 0.5-1.0 points (UltraFeedback 73.26 vs 72.21; MMLU 90.01 vs 89.32; ARMMAN 85.78 vs 85.24), t-statistics 12.5, 23.4, 3.2. ISP was the top method in only 12.5% of 16 ensembles and the best single model (91.02) beat it on MMLU; the weighted rule OW gives the large gain on hard items (MMLU-hard 24.79 vs MV 17.23). Second-order data came from answer co-occurrence, not from asked-for predictions.
agent_test: Compare majority, plain SP and a first-order-plus-second-order weighted vote on the same sample set.

claim: Ratio scoring inside one model (MaxRatio, an SP-like likelihood ratio) helps on TruthfulQA: up to +24 points (table: +24 for 7B, +21 for 70B; text says 24 for 70B) and up to +70 on single categories; gain larger on larger models; 4-bit quantisation hurt MaxPost but not MaxRatio.
agent_test: Rank candidate answers by p(answer|question)/p(answer|generic prompt) instead of raw likelihood.

claim: Bayesian-truth-serum style voting among LLM judges did not beat majority: every variant about 1 point below majority on 871 code-review items (significant after correction), same on a 150-item probe; calibration improved (ECE down 21-32%).
agent_test: Use SP-style scores as a calibration signal rather than as the selector.

claim: Learned aggregation using confidence plus meta-prediction reached 64% success (RCR-Agg) when only 28% of respondents were individually correct (Shinitzky et al. 2022); Machine Truth Serum gains over majority vote on high-disagreement items vary widely by dataset and variant: heuristic MTS fixed 48 of 149 on Spambase (+32%) but 5 of 52 on Hill Valley (+9.8%), and discriminative MTS fixed 70 of 76 on Spambase but 1 of 64 on Hill Valley.
agent_test: On hard low-accuracy items, test learned aggregation vs majority and SP.
audit_note: Table 2 of Luo and Liu: the heuristic variant (HMTS) fixed 48 of 149 on Spambase and 5 of 52 on Hill Valley; '1 of 64' on Hill Valley is the discriminative variant (DMTS), whose Spambase result is 70 of 76, so the claim mixes variants.
claim_before_audit: Learned or truth-serum aggregation helps when the crowd is mostly wrong: ML aggregation using confidence plus meta-prediction reached 64% with only 28% individually correct; Machine Truth Serum fixed 48 of 149 high-disagreement Spambase cases (+32%) but only 1 of 64 on Hill Valley.

claim: Using honest prediction of group frequency as an RL reward reduced sycophancy: flip rate under user pressure 23% to 4%, accuracy under pressure 80% to 93% on a 3B model (synthetic items).
agent_test: Requires training; note only.

claim: Confidence weighting is not a reliable fix for LLM crowds: it hurt on HLE (majority 25.1 to 17.3 for one model) and helped on BoolQ (80.0 to 84.0 for GPT-oss-20B).
agent_test: Check confidence-vs-correctness calibration before weighting.

claim: No independent same-design replication of the 21.3% figure was found in this search. The search was incomplete (APIs rate-limited, key paper pages blocked). The known field tests (Lee 2018, Rutchick 2020) use different domains and show small or negative differences.
agent_test: Treat 21.3% as one study; do not use it as a prior for LLM gains.

claim: LLM errors are strongly correlated across models: across 349 HuggingFace models mean agreement when both are wrong is 0.423 (chance about 0.12); across 71 HELM models 0.60 (chance 1/3). More accurate models are more correlated. Same provider adds only +0.02 to +0.07 in agreement, so model-name diversity is a weak fix.
agent_test: Compute pairwise wrong-answer agreement among the scaffold's samples; log top-wrong-answer share.
audit_note: Only Kim et al. carries the numbers; the second listed source (Consensus is Not Verification) supports the general point, not these figures.

claim: Plain SP is at or below majority under independence-violating conditions: in simulation with 4 agents SP is below majority at every K from 2 to 10 (e.g. K=4 90.52 vs 92.64), and theory orders expected advantage ISP >= MV >= SP when difficulty varies across questions.
agent_test: Do not use plain SP as selector; if tested, use it only as a secondary arm.

claim: Higher-order information is better used as a weight or inverse-SP score than as the SP selector, but gains over majority are small on real LLMs (0.7 to 1.5 points) except on hard items, and no study compared cost at equal tokens.
agent_test: Arms at equal tokens: majority, SP, ISP-from-co-occurrence, confidence weight; report hard items separately.

claim: No published test was found of SP or ISP with a current reasoning model against self-consistency at equal token cost. Self-consistency gave +3.9 to +17.9 points over greedy CoT on 2022 models, so SP-type gains of about one point are second-order.
agent_test: Run the equal-token test on HTSA benchmarks; this is the main open experiment.

claim: Verbalised meta-prediction in LLM crowds (Consensus paper) tracks the vote share, so it probably mirrors the model's own consensus; no study found measures whether it carries signal beyond the sample's own vote. Models also lean toward popular options (66% popular-wrong in the hardest setting).
agent_test: Log predicted share and own answer per sample; test whether prediction residuals predict correctness.

claim: For open-ended and many-option answers, no SP or ISP study handles clustering. Ai et al. list open-ended weights as future work; Goel scores a fixed candidate list (mean 7.6) with a likelihood ratio against a question-free prior.
agent_test: Cluster final answers by normalised form first, then apply any rule over clusters.

claim: Model diversity helps ensembles: in a forecasting budget study the best 5-sample mix used four different models rather than one. Pooling five models across three families did not restore independence for SP. No persona study was found.
agent_test: If a crowd is used, vary model or prompt family; personas are an untested arm.

claim: Two-round voting (see the tally, then vote again) contains SP as a special case. In LLM hiring simulations DeepSeek R1 rose from 0.56 to 0.88 under biased signals while GPT-4o stayed at 0.50 to 0.48.
agent_test: Optional: a second pass that sees the first-pass tally; effect is model-dependent.
